subject: axolotl
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: axolotl with frilly pink gills.
Style: chibi.
reasoning:
I'm planning the axolotl design in chibi style, working through its distinctive features like the wide flat head, side gills, stubby limbs, and pink coloring, while thinking through how to translate these into the SDK's building blocks.

I'm sketching out the skeleton structure facing forward: a spine chain from hips through chest to a large flat head with a jaw joint, a long tail chain curving upward at the tip, four two-joint legs each with four small finger digits, and six gill stalk chains (three per side) made of two or three joints each, all while keeping total joint count under the 160 limit.

For the color palette, I'm picking pale pink for the body, a lighter shade for the belly, hot pink with lighter tips for the gills, and dark eyes with a soft blush. I'm considering whether to use the toon kit's cel shading or anime eye components for the chibi look, but since real axolotl eyes are tiny side dots, I think drawing my own simple SVG eye with a large black oval and highlight dots gives me more control than the preset anime eye style.

I'm layering paint functions -- mottled speckles, then countershading, then cel shading -- to build a textured, toon-shaded skin, and sizing the head as a wide, flattened sphere scaled larger than the body for that chibi proportion.

Now I'm nailing down the actual coordinates: body resting low with belly near the floor, a stubby rounded torso, and the head positioned above and slightly forward with gills sweeping outward and upward from the back of the head.

For the spine, I'm planning two chains that meet at the hips — one running forward into the neck, the other running backward and curving into a tapering tail — so I can sweep the whole body as a single continuous surface over this bone list.

For the tail I'm thinking it should be laterally compressed into a fin shape, with radii tapering differently in x and y to make it tall and thin, and I'm adding a membrane lifted along the surface normal to create a raised fin ridge on top.

Instead of a constant-height fin that would stick out past the tail tip, I need to taper it — building the fin outline from sampled points along the tail's curved path so its height shrinks toward the end.

Working out the outline math...

I'll close the tip simply with top slightly above and bottom slightly below the endpoint. For the tail fin's start near the hips, I'll let it begin tucked inside the body radius so it reads as a natural dorsal extension rather than a hard seam, rising up gradually as it goes.

I'm now thinking about rigging — whether the fin should stay rigid to the hips or get split into segments so it can bend naturally with the tail joints instead of staying stiff.

I'll skip the dorsal ridge detail and just start the fin membrane from the hips, using thin rows with a subtle thickness and a paint gradient blending the base pink to a deeper pink toward the fin's edge.

Now I'm defining the tail path with catmull-rom curves following the bone chain, sweeping a tapered tube along it with radius functions that shrink toward the tip, while adding mottled spots to the fin's paint pattern.

For the body I'm setting up the spine chain with hip-to-shoulder control points, sweeping a chunky tapered tube with its own radius curve, and matching up the rear section's cap where the tail tube attaches.

Still placing joints and shapes...

I'm shaping the head using scaled spheres for the cranium and a separate lower jaw piece, positioning them with a jaw joint pivot so the mouth line sits where cranium and jaw meet.

Decided instead to use decals for the smile, pink cheek blush, and widely-spaced chibi eyes placed on the top-front of the head, angled outward-forward-up so they read as looking toward the viewer.

Reconsidering reliability, I'm weighing a sphere-plus-highlight eye construction instead of decals, and exploring using surface hit detection around the head center with azimuth/elevation angles to place the eyes precisely at the correct outward-facing normal.

Now I'm figuring out the mouth decal: applying it to the combined skull and jaw surface, placing a smile near the front where the jaw meets the skull, and working out the azimuth/elevation angle and width needed so the curve wraps naturally around the curved face.

For nostrils, I'm planning to stick two tiny dark spheres near the top of the snout rather than use a decal, placing them symmetrically at a small azimuth offset and elevation.

Now I'm adding pink blush ellipses on the cheeks with a lighter tone and a few small stripe details for a chibi effect, then tackling the gills — the signature feature — as three stalks per side emerging from the back of the head, curving outward and upward, each with feathery filament fringe along the stalk.

I'm placing filament pairs at angles along each stalk using surface-normal frames, tapering their length from base to tip for a feathery look—roughly 108 small cone-shaped parts total across six gill stalks, which feels like a lot to budget for.

I'm giving each filament a color gradient from deep pink near the root to a lighter shade at the tip using banded color stops, and considering whether to curve them with bezier sweeps instead of straight spikes for a more organic shape.

Now I'm positioning the gill stalks against the skull geometry, defining a center point with radii for the head and placing three stalk pairs per side using azimuth and elevation angles across the back and side of the skull.

Computing stalk directions and curve points...

Still writing filament placement logic...

Working out spike's base and direction parameters, combining the frame's normal and tangent vectors into a single direction vector for the taper, and setting the radius profile from base to tip.

With roughly 144 spikes across all stalks at low poly counts each, the triangle budget stays manageable. I'm fattening the filaments slightly for a fluffier chibi look and settling on a pink gradient from root to tip, plus matching stalk colors.

For textures I'm aiming for the 5-12 range, planning eye, smile, blush decals, and adding a scatter of small dark pink speckles across the back for that leucistic axolotl look. Now I'm working out leg placement and proportions—short stubby chibi legs with the front pair anchored near the shoulder and angled outward and down.

For the limb poses I'm figuring out the front legs' sprawl: root and target positions, segment lengths, and bend hints so the elbow bends naturally upward and back when the limb reaches out to the side.

For the hind legs, I'm setting similar root/target coordinates and a forward-up knee bend, then naming joint chains (shoulder/elbow/wrist per side) and parenting them to the spine or hips, sweeping each limb with tapered radii for a tube-like shape.

For the feet, I'm going with webbed axolotl digits—four slender fingers per foot, each built as a single capsule from palm to tip with a small rounded radius, attached to a single digit joint parented to the wrist tip, plus a tiny bulbous sphere at each fingertip for a cute rounded look.

I'm fanning each finger outward from the wrist position at angles spread roughly between -36° and 36° around the vertical axis, keeping them flat near the floor with a short length and small tip radius so they read as delicate little toes.

I'm adjusting the vertical placement of the palm pad, fingers, and tips so they just barely touch the floor without clipping through it, then setting up each digit as a joint aimed from its base toward its tip. I'm also noting that the hind feet need five toes versus four on the front, matching real axolotl anatomy.

I'm tallying up the total joint count across gills, spine, tail, head, limbs, and fingers to get a rough sense of the rig's complexity, landing around sixty joints. For extra charm I'm considering cream countershading on the belly and cheek frills, while skipping things like eyelids or a head crest, and double-checking that the jaw and body sit flush with the floor without any gaps.

Still tuning body-part coordinates...

Working out the fin membrane shape now, tapering from a small base near the body to a rounded tip using a sine-based curve for smooth growth and falloff.

I realize a bottom fin would poke below the floor, so I'm dropping the ventral fin and keeping only the top fin, with the bottom edge pulled inward along the tail tube instead. Now I'm sizing the tail tube radius at its base.

Defining paint colors...

I'm thinking about small decorative touches—eyes with ink outlines, maybe tiny gill-base rings and skin speckles via scatter—while keeping the module reasonably compact rather than padding it out unnecessarily.

Now I'm working out the skull geometry sizing and how it meets the jaw sphere, making sure the mouth seam lines up correctly between the two scaled parts and that the head paint continues the same mottled texture as the body for visual continuity.

I'm placing the jaw joint relative to the head and adjusting the head's own joint position and forward direction so the hierarchy aims correctly.

For the spine, I'm defining three joint names (spine1-3) across the control points, with the head parented to the spine's tip joint and hips rooting the chain. For the tail, I'm setting up four joint names across the five control points to form the spans.

Now I'm thinking through the skinning: sweeping the spine chain with a radius function that varies by t, tapering slightly larger near the head end and hidden under the head's cap, while the body color fills the sweep.

I'm scattering small pink spot cylinders across the body, filtered to avoid overlapping the eye decals on the head, then planning the limb sweeps with radii that taper from upper arm to hand.

Now I'm checking shoulder and foot placement for the limb geometry, then working through the limb function's signature to figure out how the bend directions for the elbow joint should be passed in.

I'm setting up the arm chain with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints, naming them with left/right suffixes. For the front-left arm, I'm computing the direction from shoulder to target and figuring out how the bend hint should angle the elbow upward so it bends naturally outward and back.

Now I'm doing the same geometry for the hind leg chain, setting root and target positions with left/right mirroring and defining segment lengths.

Then I shift focus to finger placement on the hand, having fingers extend outward from the palm pad along a direction vector, working out the angular spread for the front paw.

Still writing finger joints...

For the arm sweep, eyes via decals, and gill details I'm adding a base bump sphere at each gill root colored to match, then starting to code the gill array with hit points on the skull surface.

Now I'm working out the vector math to position each gill: finding the surface hit point, computing a direction vector, and building a point path for the gill's sweep starting from that location and extending outward.

Still writing sprout logic...

Setting spike size with slight tapering and overlap for a fluffy effect, leaning each spike along a blend of normal and tangent direction. Now I'm positioning the eyes on the skull using azimuth and elevation angles, computing a direction vector and scaling it against the ellipsoid dimensions to place them high and wide on the front-top of the head for that chibi look.

Working out the eye SVG with layered ellipses: a dark outer shape, a deep purple inner ring, and bright highlight circles positioned off-center for a glossy, big-eyed effect.

Now I'm placing the blush marks on the cheeks, picking a soft pink that sits below and outward from the eyes so it doesn't overlap the gill roots, and checking its position relative to the mouth corners.

For the smile, I'm drawing a curved stroke path with rounded ends and thick enough width to stay visible at the decal texture resolution, plus small tick marks at the corners for cheek dimples. I'm then placing this smile decal onto the skull and jaw meshes, working out the exact z-depth so it lands right at the front surface where the two parts meet.

Adding jaw placement, then placing tiny nostril dots near the snout top-front using skull azimuth/elevation coordinates, and double-checking that skull's `.at` position can serve as the center reference for the chibi's floating extras.

Skipping gill feather cards since the spikes already provide enough frill, but I'm adding freckle-like spots via stick placement and considering a sparkle texture for the eyes. For the fin paint, I'm blending pink toward a brighter edge color based on vertical position along the fin using a smoothstep gradient.

Now I'm setting up the TypeScript export structure with vector helpers and rotation utilities, then writing the hand-building function that places palm spheres and positions fingers at angles around a base point.

I'm confirming that giving a chain three joint names (shoulder, elbow, wrist) means the wrist becomes the tip joint, since three points yield two spans plus a tip. Now I'm setting up the sweep for the arm bone shape using those joint names with a tapering radius.

For the chibi's decals, like blush and eye placement, I need a helper that samples the skull surface at a given azimuth and elevation to get a hit point for positioning. Writing surface sampling helper...

Then I'm scattering spot decals across the body tube and tail, filtering by surface normal to keep them on visible faces, with slight color variation between spots for visual interest.

I decide against toe webbing, settle on the spot color and gill filament gradients (dark roots to lighter tips, deep pink stalk base fading toward a brighter hue), and confirm gills stay in their rest-pose extended position before writing out the final assembled code.

Writing creature generation code...

Building the tail fin chain, using control points to curve it along the hips...

I'm checking the taper radii against the curve's y-values at each parameter t, verifying the sweep matches the intended silhouette width at the base, quarter, and midpoint.

Now I'm computing the fin top and bottom edges along the tail path, offsetting each point by the local radius and a sine-based taper factor to shape the fin profile.

I'm building the membrane between the fin edges using Catmull-Rom splines through both point sets, then starting to define the spine points for the main body.

I'm defining the spine as a chain of 3 points with 2 spans, considering whether hips should be a separate root joint or part of the spine chain's role classification.

Now I'm adding the head joint parented to the spine tip with its direction and position, then attaching the jaw with its own aim target. I'm setting up a tube radius function along the spine's parameter and confirming it matches the expected endpoint radius, then deciding legs should parent to hips while arms parent to a spine joint partway up.

I'm placing symmetric eye decals on the skull using mirrored offsets, with a small highlight detail, then moving on to add blush decals for extra character.

For the gill filaments, I'm checking the root placements on the back of the ellipsoid so they align with the body curve, and setting up the spike call for each filament to taper from a root color to a tip color along its length, keeping just the band gradient rather than a flat color.

Spikes should sit right on the surface at each sweep point, using the point's normal and tangent to orient the cone direction; I'll skip trying to embed the base inward since that would lose the bone inheritance, so they'll just start flush with the surface.

For the fingertip color I'm using a soft pink, and I'm double-checking that rng usage for scatter looks consistent before moving to the actual SVGs.

Writing SVG code...

Writing the smile curve and blush ellipse markup...

Now I'm checking the limb-building helper's API — making sure bend arguments and joint points pass as single values or flat arrays correctly, and confirming the chain function accepts a polyline of Vector3 points for straight limb segments.

Writing character skeleton code...
